n: Continuing the promises of chapter 30: in that coming day, God will be the God of all Israel’s families—north and south reunited—and they will be his people.
God recalls the Exodus: the people who survived the sword found grace in the wilderness when he led Israel toward rest. What he did once, he will do again.
“I have loved you with an everlasting love; that’s why I have drawn you to me with unfailing kindness.” God’s love, not Israel’s merit, is the root of restoration.

f.w: I have loved thee with an everlasting love

f.g: Hebrew chesed—loyal, covenant love that keeps faith.

n: God will rebuild “virgin Israel.” She will again pick up her tambourines and join the joyful dances.

f.g: Small hand drums or tambourines.

n: Vineyards will be planted again on Samaria’s hills, and the planters will enjoy the fruit themselves. Under the law, a new vineyard’s fruit had to wait several years before ordinary use—here peace lasts long enough to enjoy it.

f.g: Use the fruit freely after the waiting period.

n: Watchmen in the northern hills of Ephraim will call, “Come, let’s go up to Zion to the Lord!” The old split between north and south will be healed in worship.

f.w: let us go up to Zion

f.g: The central hill country of the former northern kingdom.

n: Sing and shout for Jacob among the nations! Proclaim, praise, and pray, “Lord, save your people, the remnant of Israel.”

f.g: Israel—the foremost of nations in God’s plan.

n: God will bring them from the north and from the ends of the earth—including the blind, the lame, and pregnant women. No one is too weak to be included in the gathering.

f.w: I will bring them from the north country

n: They will come weeping and praying, and God will lead them beside streams on a smooth road. He is a father to Israel, and Ephraim is his firstborn. Latter-day Saints note Ephraim’s special role in the latter-day gathering.
Announce it to the nations and distant coastlands: the God who scattered Israel will gather and protect them as a shepherd guards his flock.

f.w: as a shepherd doth his flock

n: The Lord has redeemed and ransomed Jacob from a stronger power—language of buying back a family member from slavery. Latter-day Saints see in this the redemption Jesus Christ offers.

f.g: Hebrew padah and ga’al—to ransom, to buy back as a near kinsman.

n: They will sing on Zion’s heights and stream toward God’s goodness—grain, wine, oil, and flocks. Their lives will be like a well-watered garden, with no more sorrow.

f.g: Stream like a river—or be radiant with joy.

n: Young women will dance, and young and old men will celebrate together. God will turn their mourning into joy and comfort them.

f.w: I will turn their mourning into joy

n: Priests will have abundant offerings to share, and God’s people will be fully satisfied with his goodness.

f.g: Richness, abundance—the best portions of offerings.

n: A haunting image: Rachel, mother of Joseph and Benjamin, weeps in Ramah for her lost children. Ramah was likely where exiles were gathered before being marched to Babylon. Matthew applies this verse to Herod’s slaughter of the children of Bethlehem.

f.g: A town about 5 miles north of Jerusalem, near Rachel’s tomb tradition.

n: God answers Rachel tenderly: stop weeping; your labor will be rewarded, and your children will come back from the enemy’s land.
There is hope for your future: your children will return home.

f.w: there is hope in thine end

n: God has heard Ephraim (the northern tribes) mourning: “You disciplined me like an untrained calf. Turn me back, and I will return—you are my God.” Repentance begins by asking God for help to change.

f.g: An untrained young ox that resists the yoke.

f.w: turn thou me, and I shall be turned

n: Ephraim continues: after I turned back, I repented; once I understood, I struck my thigh in grief and felt the shame of my youthful sins.

f.g: A gesture of grief and remorse.

n: God’s tender response: “Isn’t Ephraim my dear son, my delight? Even when I speak against him, I still remember him. My heart yearns for him—I will surely have mercy.” One of the most moving pictures of God as a loving Father.

f.w: my bowels are troubled for him
f.g: Bowels = the inner self, seat of deep emotion—“my heart aches for him.”

n: Set up road markers and signposts! Remember the road you took into exile, and come back along it, virgin Israel, to your cities.

f.g: Road markers, signposts.
Piles of stones as guideposts.

n: How long will you wander, unfaithful daughter? God has created something new on earth: “a woman shall encompass a man.” The meaning is debated—perhaps a reversal in which faithful Israel (the woman) now embraces or seeks the Lord, or protects her own.

f.w: A woman shall compass a man
f.g: Compass = surround, encircle. A cryptic proverb; scholars propose many explanations.
Turning away, unfaithful.

n: When God restores Judah, people will again bless Jerusalem: “The Lord bless you, home of righteousness, holy mountain.”
Farmers and shepherds will live together peacefully in Judah’s towns.

f.g: Farmers.

n: God will refresh the weary and fill every sorrowful soul.

f.w: I have satiated the weary soul

n: Jeremiah wakes up—this message may have come in a dream or vision—and for once his sleep was sweet. After so many grim messages, this one brought peace.
Days are coming when God will “sow” Israel and Judah with people and animals—repopulating the empty land.
Just as God watched over them to uproot and tear down, now he will watch over them to build and plant—the words of Jeremiah’s original call, now turned fully to hope.
People will stop quoting the proverb, “The parents ate sour grapes, but the children’s teeth are set on edge”—blaming their troubles on their ancestors.

f.w: The fathers have eaten a sour grape

f.g: Made raw and sensitive, as by sour fruit.

n: Instead each person will be accountable for his own sin. This is a principle Latter-day Saints affirm: we are punished for our own sins, not for Adam’s or our parents’.

f.w: every one shall die for his own iniquity

n: One of the great prophecies of scripture: God will make a “new covenant” with Israel and Judah. The phrase “new covenant” (new testament) gave the New Testament its name.
It won’t be like the Sinai covenant made when God led them out of Egypt by the hand, which they broke even though he was like a husband to them.

f.w: I was an husband unto them
f.g: Some ancient versions read “I disregarded them” (quoted that way in Hebrews 8:9).

n: In the new covenant, God will write his law on their hearts, not just on stone tablets. Obedience will come from inside—a changed nature. This is the “mighty change of heart” the Book of Mormon describes.

f.g: Innermost being.

n: Everyone, from least to greatest, will personally know the Lord, and he will forgive sins and remember them no more. Personal revelation and complete forgiveness through Christ are at the heart of this promise.

f.w: I will remember their sin no more

n: The God who makes this promise is the one who set the sun, moon, and stars in their places and controls the roaring sea.

f.g: Fixed laws, set order.

f.w: which divideth the sea when the waves thereof roar

n: Only if those laws of nature fail would Israel ever stop being a nation before God. His covenant is as reliable as the sunrise.
If anyone could measure the heavens or explore the earth’s foundations, only then would God reject all of Israel’s descendants. In other words—never.

f.w: I will also cast off all the seed of Israel

n: Jerusalem will be rebuilt for the Lord, from the Tower of Hananel in the north to the Corner Gate in the west.
The surveyor’s line will extend further to the hill of Gareb and around to Goath—places whose exact locations are now unknown, probably on the west and southwest.

Even the Valley of Hinnom—full of corpses and ashes of sacrifices—and the fields down to the Kidron will become holy to the Lord, never to be destroyed again. The most defiled place will be made holy.

f.w: the whole valley of the dead bodies

f.g: The valley east of Jerusalem, between the city and the Mount of Olives.
